query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy-alloy multilayers, a modulation period of 16 nm creates semicoherent FCC/BCC interfaces that strongly block dislocation glide, causing local dislocation pileup and high stress, which in turn triggers interfacial amorphization. This amorphization promotes atomic diffusion or interface slip, allowing a transition from dislocation-mediated creep to a rate-limited creep mechanism that improves room-temperature creep resistance compared to multilayers with either coherent interfaces (8 nm) or grain-boundary-dominated structures (32/80 nm).
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, approximately 1 μm-thick FCC/BCC Al-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings produced from Al0.2CrFeNi and Al targets.
generation.intervention: Vary the modulation period (individual layer thickness, λ) among 8, 16, 32, and 80 nm via RF magnetron sputtering to obtain multilayers with different interface characters, followed by room-temperature nanoindentation creep testing.
generation.conditions: Deposition parameters include a base pressure of about 5×10^-4 Pa, Ar flow of 100 sccm, working pressure of 0.3 Pa, 150 W on the HEA target with alternating 0/30 W on the Al target for 1 hour. Nanoindentation creep testing is done at room temperature with 5 mN maximum load, loading rates of 1, 0.1, and 0.01 mN/s, a 100 s hold period, and 20 s unloading, with indentation depths maintained at roughly 1/10–1/7 of the coating thickness.
generation.structural_mediator: Interface coherency. The 16 nm multilayers exhibit semicoherent FCC/BCC interfaces (with misfit dislocations) that promote localized high stresses and potential interfacial amorphization, in contrast to fully coherent interfaces in 8 nm multilayers or grain-boundary-dominated structures in 32/80 nm samples.
generation.mechanism: Semicoherent interfaces block dislocation glide, leading to dislocation pileup and localized stress concentrations. Under sustained loading, this may trigger stress-induced interfacial amorphization. The resulting free volume, structural disorder, and high-energy crystal–amorphous boundaries lower atomic-migration barriers, enabling a shift from dislocation slip/climb to atomic-diffusion or interface-slip controlled creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: The 16 nm (semicoherent) multilayer will demonstrate the highest room-temperature creep resistance and a transition to a lower creep stress exponent (indicative of diffusion/interface-slip-controlled creep, n around 1–2) compared to the 8 nm coherent-interface and 32/80 nm grain-boundary-dominated multilayers, which will exhibit higher creep stress exponents (n > 3) indicative of dislocation-mediated creep.
generation.baseline: The baseline behavior is defined by the 8 nm multilayer (coherent interfaces with continuous atomic planes) and the 32/80 nm multilayers (grain-boundary-dominated), both of which exhibit predominantly dislocation-mediated creep.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to the studied high-entropy-alloy multilayers at room temperature under nanoindentation creep testing with a maximum load of 5 mN, where the total coating thickness is approximately 1 μm and the deformation mechanisms are assessed within indentation depths of roughly 1/10–1/7 of the coating thickness.
generation.uncertainty: The direct observation of stress-induced interfacial amorphization under sustained loading remains partially unverified, and further microscopy (e.g., in situ TEM) would be needed to fully confirm this process.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multilayers with λ = 8, 16, 32, and 80 nm as described. Use X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT) to characterize interface coherency and check for signs of amorphization under loading. Conduct nanoindentation creep tests at room temperature (with maximum 5 mN load, varying loading rates, and defined hold and unloading periods) to obtain load–displacement and displacement–dwell-time curves. Perform linear regression on ln(strain rate) versus ln(flow stress) to extract the creep stress exponent (n).
measurements: XRD and TEM/IFFT for phase identification and interface character (coherent, semicoherent, or grain boundary).
Load–displacement curves and displacement–dwell-time measurements from nanoindentation creep tests.
Creep stress exponent measurement from ln(strain rate) vs ln(flow stress) plots to distinguish between diffusion/interface-slip creep (n ≈ 1–2) and dislocation-mediated creep (n > 3).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 16 nm multilayer does not show a lower creep stress exponent (n closer to 1–2) and the highest creep resistance relative to the 8 nm and 32/80 nm samples, or if no evidence of interfacial amorphization is observed under sustained loading, then the proposed hypothesis is falsified.
